title: Elite schools, magnet classes, and academic performances: Regression-discontinuity evidence from China
supported_claim: Magnet-class enrollment raised borderline students' college entrance examination scores by 0.435 standard deviations. Decomposition estimates teacher effects at about 40-42% of peer effects; peer effects are estimated at approximately 0.31 SD.
limitations: The study uses RD evidence from one poor rural county in Hunan and evaluates students near admission cutoffs. The teacher/peer split is a decomposition/calculation, not an independently randomized causal decomposition. The proposed 30/70 allocation is a reasonable rounding of peer ~70%, teachers ~30%, but paper wording reports teacher effect as 40-42% of peer effect (not 30/70 of total).

title: Private Tutoring Before and After the ‘Double-Reduction’ Policy in China: Choices and Rationale
supported_claim: Mixed-method study reports questionnaires from 486 parents and follow-up interviews with 23 parents in Guangzhou; examines tutoring choices before/after Double Reduction and SES associations.
limitations: One primary/secondary school in Guangzhou, parent-reported retrospective comparisons, and no causal identification of policy effects. Article uses article pagination rather than conventional issue page span. The accessible copy is author manuscript hosted by Cardiff; metadata/title and DOI match SAGE record.

title: Parental heuristics and demand for private tutoring: continuities amidst changes brought by China’s double-reduction policy
supported_claim: Bibliographic record confirms the stated authors/year/volume and article concerns parental heuristics and tutoring demand across Double Reduction.
limitations: The accessible record confirms publication metadata and topic; the full text was not reviewed in this pass, so detailed empirical claims should not be attributed without checking the publisher article.

title: Regulating Private Tutoring: Human Capital Formation, Inequality, and Intergenerational Mobility
supported_claim: Article constructs a quantitative partial-equilibrium OLG model, calibrated to Chinese microdata, comparing a complete ban, imperfectly enforced ban/black-market access, and a tutoring tax. The paper itself characterizes its policy results as model-based and conditional, not a causal evaluation of the observed Double Reduction reform.
limitations: Published 17 September 2026 per publisher, so temporal fit depends on manuscript cutoff. Claims are simulations under assumptions; access-cost ordering is assumed and it is partial equilibrium. Model calibration uses CFPS 2010-2022.

title: Taming the Wild Horse of Shadow Education: The Global Expansion of Private Tutoring and Regulatory Responses
supported_claim: Publisher verifies title, author, 2023 copyright, first edition, and global/regulatory scope.
limitations: Book-level metadata only; cite specific chapters/pages for substantive claims.

title: Timescapes of shadow education: patterns and forces in the temporal features of private supplementary tutoring
supported_claim: Publisher title/author/DOI verified; article applies timescapes lens to temporal features of private supplementary tutoring.
limitations: Publisher metadata may show online-first 2022 and a later issue assignment; verify final volume/issue/pages from publisher before supplying complete issue citation.

title: Agent-Based Simulation Models of the College Sorting Process
journal: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation
supported_claim: Official JASSS page confirms article metadata and describes agent-based modeling of socioeconomic resources and college sorting.
limitations: Stylized simulation, not empirical causal estimate; relevance should be restricted to sorting mechanism/modeling.

title: Equalization or Selection? Reassessing the ‘Meritocratic Power’ of a College Degree in Intergenerational Income Mobility
supported_claim: Paper argues college graduation can act as a collider for origins and unobserved ability in analyses of intergenerational mobility; adjustment/conditioning can distort observed equalization patterns.
limitations: The paper concerns college completion and income mobility in U.S. data; do not generalize as a direct estimate of tutoring/school sorting in China.

title: Magnet high schools and academic performance in China: A regression discontinuity design
supported_claim: Verified bibliographic details; RD study investigates high-school quality effects using entrance exam thresholds, finding increased college attainment from magnet high school attendance.
limitations: Evidence from rural counties in western China and high school admission; not directly interchangeable with urban magnet-class or private-tutoring effects.

title: The achievement and course-taking effects of magnet schools: Regression-discontinuity evidence from urban China
supported_claim: Bibliographic record confirms urban China RD study of magnet schools, achievement, and course taking.
limitations: This is magnet-school research, not a private supplementary tutoring evaluation.

title: Unresolved from author-year alone; likely a magnet/elite school study, but multiple distinct Zhang 2016 works exist
supported_claim: No unique bibliographic record can be safely matched from ‘Zhang 2016’ alone. A 2019 paper by Wu et al. cites Zhang (2016) as finding little positive academic benefit of elite-school attendance in a provincial capital, but this does not establish the intended source identity.
limitations: Needs full first name/title or reference-list context before citation.
